paragraphs: Discrete diffusion models generate discrete data through a process governed by transition rates. Experiments have often favored absorbing rate matrices over uniform ones, but the corresponding theory has lagged behind. This paper develops finite-time error bounds and convergence rates for the absorbing case, giving mathematical support to a class of models already showing empirical promise.

A central difficulty is that the absorbing process concentrates its stationary distribution on a single state. This makes the KL-divergence comparison needed for the analysis ill-defined. The authors introduce a surrogate initialization distribution and derive an upper bound for the forward process, creating a way to analyze convergence despite that concentration.

The analysis establishes guarantees for both tau-leaping and uniformization samplers, with improved rates relative to their uniform-rate counterparts. Under suitable assumptions, it also establishes convergence without early stopping. New bounds on score functions near initialization help make that result possible. These are guarantees about convergence and approximation error; the reported rate improvements provide a theoretical comparison rather than a new empirical claim about generation quality.
neurips-2025-absorb-and-converge-provabl.tldr: The paper establishes convergence and finite-time error guarantees for absorbing discrete diffusion, including guarantees without early stopping under suitable assumptions.

paragraphs: Fine-tuning a large model efficiently requires deciding which parts of its parameters should change for a new task. AdaMSS approaches this decision by dividing the space of weight updates into several smaller subspaces. During training, it progressively reduces the trainable parameters, eventually concentrating updates in a small subset of subspaces relevant to the downstream task.

This adaptive segmentation gives the method a finer way to allocate its limited trainable capacity than methods that work within one large subspace. The approach uses lowest-rank representations to keep updates compact. The paper also presents theoretical analysis giving AdaMSS a better generalization guarantee than LoRA, PiSSA, and other single-subspace low-rank methods.

Across image classification, language understanding, and language generation, the authors report performance comparable to full fine-tuning and better than other parameter-efficient methods in most cases. On ViT-Large, they report 4.7% higher average accuracy than LoRA using 15.4% as many trainable parameters. On RoBERTa-Large, the reported improvement over PiSSA is 7%, with approximately 94.4% fewer trainable parameters. These results support adapting where updates occur as well as limiting their size.
neurips-2025-adamss-adaptive-multi-subsp.tldr: AdaMSS adaptively concentrates fine-tuning in task-relevant subspaces, reporting strong performance with substantially fewer trainable parameters.

paragraphs: Chip placement determines where modules sit on a chip, with consequences for the completed design's performance, power use, and area. Because the full design workflow takes considerable time, placement algorithms are often evaluated using faster intermediate measurements. The problem is that improvements in these surrogate measurements may not correspond to improvements in the finished chip.

ChiPBench evaluates AI-based placement methods using final design outcomes. Its evaluation dataset covers 20 circuits from domains including CPUs, GPUs, and NPUs. The authors apply six state-of-the-art AI placement algorithms and analyze their placement behavior alongside the resulting performance, power, and area measurements.

The experiments find unsatisfactory final results from the evaluated algorithms and highlight the influence of factors such as regularity and dataflow. This makes the benchmark useful for examining whether a placement method's apparent progress survives the rest of the design workflow. The contribution is an evaluation framework that connects algorithm assessment more directly to engineering outcomes, with bridging academic research and industrial needs stated as an intended benefit.
neurips-2025-benchmarking-end-to-end-per.tldr: ChiPBench evaluates AI chip placement through final design outcomes and finds that the tested methods deliver unsatisfactory performance, power, and area results.

paragraphs: Generating a plausible-looking bicycle is only part of engineering a useful design. BikeBench evaluates whether generated bicycles also meet performance objectives and constraints. It brings together requirements involving physical behavior, human use, and subjective preferences, making the task broader than reproducing the appearance or statistical patterns of existing designs.

The benchmark measures characteristics including aerodynamics, ergonomics, structural mechanics, human-rated usability, and agreement with text or image prompts. Its supporting resources include simulation datasets, 10,000 human-rated bicycle assessments, and 1.6 million synthetic designs. Each synthetic design has parametric, CAD/XML, SVG, and PNG representations, supporting evaluation across different kinds of modeling systems.

BikeBench compares tabular generative models, language models, design optimization methods, and hybrid approaches within one benchmark. In the reported experiments, combinations of generative AI and optimization outperform language models and tabular generators on design quality, constraint satisfaction, and similarity scores. The findings suggest that combining generation with optimization is valuable in these tested design tasks, while exposing substantial room for improvement in constrained engineering generation.
neurips-2025-bikebench-a-bicycle-design-.tldr: BikeBench tests bicycle generation against engineering and human requirements, with hybrid generation-and-optimization methods leading the reported comparisons.

paragraphs: Formal problem-solving places a deductive solution inside a theorem-proving environment so its steps can be checked. The paper addresses two obstacles: informal reasoning and formal proofs operate at different levels of detail, and formal problem-solution training pairs are extremely scarce. Existing approaches also lose efficiency through backtracking and the propagation of errors.

The proposed Hierarchical Autoregressive Formal Reasoner, or HAR, separates drafting a solution at an informal reasoning level from proving its details. It constructs solutions sequentially with feedback at each step. A complementary pipeline, CoPA, produces training data by cascading statement autoformalization, proof drafting, and proof search. Together, the pipelines address both how solutions are built and where training examples come from.

After training on data generated through CoPA, HAR raises reported performance from 15.50% to 44.09% on FormalMath500 and from 21.87% to 56.58% on MiniF2F-Solving, while using a lower computational budget. These results support coordinating hierarchical reasoning with generated formal training data. Additional explorations identify promising directions in pruning formal solutions and cleaning informal datasets.
neurips-2025-bootstrapping-hierarchical-.tldr: HAR combines hierarchical formal reasoning with CoPA-generated training data, substantially improving reported benchmark performance with a lower computational budget.

paragraphs: Evaluating medical language models requires distinguishing harmful requests from legitimate questions that happen to sound unusual. CARES builds a healthcare-specific safety benchmark around this distinction. It addresses gaps in earlier refusal evaluations by incorporating clinical safety principles, different degrees of potential harm, and attempts to bypass safeguards through changes in wording or presentation.

The benchmark contains more than 18,000 prompts spanning eight medical safety principles and four harm levels. It uses direct, indirect, obfuscated, and role-play prompting styles across malicious and benign cases. Responses are evaluated through three categories—accept, caution, and refuse—alongside a fine-grained Safety Score. This gives the evaluation more room to distinguish appropriate caution from outright refusal.

The analysis finds both vulnerability to subtly rephrased harmful prompts and excessive refusal of safe, atypically phrased questions. These results show why refusal frequency alone cannot describe the desired behavior. The authors also propose a lightweight classifier that detects jailbreak attempts and supplies safety reminders to guide the model, connecting the benchmark to a concrete mitigation strategy.
neurips-2025-cares-comprehensive-evaluat.tldr: CARES evaluates medical LLM safety across varied harms and prompt styles, revealing both jailbreak vulnerability and excessive refusal of safe questions.

paragraphs: Neural scaling laws usually relate model performance to resources such as compute, parameter count, or training data. This paper instead asks how performance changes as the problem itself becomes more complex. It studies two measures of complexity: the size of the solution space and the size of the representation space.

The Traveling Salesman Problem provides the case study. By increasing the number of nodes or spatial dimensions while keeping model size fixed, the authors examine how far solutions fall short of optimality. They find smooth trends in solution cost, allowing meaningful scaling relationships even when there is no interpretable training loss to use as the performance measure.

The reported suboptimality trends occur with both reinforcement learning and supervised fine-tuning on a static dataset. The paper also compares these patterns with local search, where a much simpler gradient descent procedure produces similar trends. This suggests that the observed scaling patterns are useful for understanding the tested problems across different solution procedures, rather than being tied exclusively to one neural training method.
neurips-2025-complexity-scaling-laws-for.tldr: Using the Traveling Salesman Problem, the paper finds predictable performance degradation as problem complexity increases for fixed-size neural models.

paragraphs: Agents may need to complete tasks while obeying limits that apply across their entire sequence of actions, such as resource budgets or safety requirements. Enforcing the final constraints from the beginning can make learning difficult. This paper proposes starting with easier constraints and gradually tightening them until training reaches the intended deployment conditions.

The curriculum gives the agent a sequence of increasingly demanding versions of the task. A theoretical analysis in a binary-tree Markov Decision Process shows that this strategy can accelerate training compared with imposing the full trajectory constraints immediately. That result supports the curriculum within the analyzed setting, while experiments examine its usefulness more broadly.

The empirical evaluation includes reinforcement learning and language-model agents in a binary-tree environment, multi-task navigation, and mathematical reasoning on two benchmarks. For language models, the method compresses the output chain-of-thought tokens and produces a substantial inference speedup on consumer hardware. The results connect gradual constraint tightening to both learning performance and the practical cost of operating an agent under a limited budget.
neurips-2025-curriculum-design-for-traje.tldr: Gradually tightening training constraints helps agents meet deployment requirements and enables shorter LLM reasoning outputs with reported inference speedups.

paragraphs: Foundation-model training depends heavily on which examples enter the dataset. Common curation approaches adjust broad mixtures of data or apply manually designed filtering rules. DataRater instead learns to estimate the training value of individual examples, making data selection a learned component of the training process rather than only a set of human choices.

The method uses meta-learning with meta-gradients. Its objective is to improve training efficiency on held-out data, so the signal for judging an example comes from the training outcome the system is trying to improve. This connects example selection to measured learning usefulness and supports finer-grained decisions than treating a large bucket of data as uniformly valuable.

Across experiments involving different model scales and datasets, filtering with DataRater significantly improves compute efficiency. The stated finding supports learned curation as a practical way to make training resources more productive in the evaluated settings. Its broader contribution is a framework for learning which data to retain, with held-out training efficiency providing the objective that guides those judgments.
neurips-2025-datarater-meta-learned-data.tldr: DataRater learns the training value of individual examples and improves compute efficiency by using those estimates to filter datasets.

paragraphs: Synthetic images could expand scarce medical training datasets, but medically inaccurate images can worsen diagnostic models. MAGIC addresses this problem for skin disease images by combining expert-defined clinical criteria with AI feedback. Its focus is on preserving the disease information that makes a generated image useful for training.

The framework breaks expert knowledge into attribute-level checklists that general-purpose multimodal language models can evaluate. Those assessments become actionable feedback for diffusion-based image synthesis. This approach reduces direct expert evaluation work by translating specialized knowledge into tasks suited to the evaluator's capabilities, rather than adapting the evaluator itself to every specialized medical task.

The authors report improved clinical quality, with generated outputs aligning with dermatologist assessments. Adding these images to training data improves diagnostic accuracy by a reported 9.02% on a 20-condition classification task and 13.89% in the few-shot setting. These findings link the quality of the synthetic images to downstream diagnostic performance in the evaluated tasks. The wider methodological idea is to use expert-designed evaluation criteria to guide general-purpose foundation models in specialized work.
neurips-2025-doctor-approved-generating-.tldr: MAGIC turns expert clinical criteria into AI feedback for skin-image generation, improving reported image quality and downstream diagnostic accuracy.

paragraphs: Multi-armed bandit methods learn which choices work best through repeated interaction. Historical data can help start that process, reducing the cost of learning entirely online. However, many hybrid methods assume that historical and live data have the same feedback structure and underlying distribution, even though data from different sources or changing environments may violate that assumption.

This paper develops a hybrid framework for heterogeneous offline and online data. It studies two directions of transfer: using historical numerical rewards to improve online preference-based learning, and using historical preferences to improve standard online bandits. The distinction matters because a reward for one choice and a comparison between two choices provide different forms of evidence.

For both settings, the authors design algorithms and establish tight regret bounds that match or improve existing benchmarks despite heterogeneity. Regret measures the accumulated cost of learning rather than consistently making the best choices. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets also show significant improvements over baseline algorithms, supporting the value of using historical feedback even when its form differs from live feedback.
neurips-2025-learning-across-the-gap-hyb.tldr: The paper develops hybrid bandit algorithms that transfer between historical rewards and preferences, with tight regret guarantees and improved empirical performance.

paragraphs: Optimization methods often learn from a sequence of observations whose successive elements are related. This paper studies non-convex optimization when those observations follow a Markov chain. It considers a restrictive situation: the learner has no prior knowledge or control of the chain and can access only one trajectory, rather than simulate several independent runs.

The authors first establish sample-complexity lower bounds for first-order methods that receive gradient estimates with bounded variance. These bounds describe unavoidable sampling requirements for reaching an approximately critical solution under the smoothness conditions studied. The paper gives lower bounds involving epsilon to the minus third and minus fourth powers, connecting the required accuracy to fundamental limits on learning.

It then introduces MaC-SPIDER, which uses variance reduction to achieve an order epsilon-to-the-minus-third upper bound under mean-squared smoothness. The corresponding lower-bound analysis establishes its near-optimality. The result concerns reaching approximate critical points in the stated non-convex setting. Its significance is that the improved sampling rate is achieved despite having only one uncontrolled Markovian trajectory.
neurips-2025-learning-from-a-single-mark.tldr: MaC-SPIDER achieves near-optimal sampling complexity for non-convex optimization from a single uncontrolled Markovian trajectory under the stated smoothness conditions.

paragraphs: Language-model safeguards must contend with jailbreak strategies that change after deployment. Training only against a fixed collection of known attacks leaves the challenge of adapting to newly developed ones. This paper proposes lifelong safety alignment, framing adaptation as an ongoing competition between a system that discovers attacks and a model that learns to resist them.

The framework pairs a Meta-Attacker with a Defender. To initialize the attacker, the authors use the GPT-4o API to extract insights from a large collection of jailbreak research papers. Iterative training then develops the attacker's strategies while improving the defender's resistance, making new attacks part of the training process.

The first attacker iteration reaches a 73% attack success rate on RR and a 57% transfer success rate on LAT using single-turn attacks. As training continues, the defender reduces the Meta-Attacker's success rate to 7%. These results demonstrate improved resistance within the reported competitive training setup and support continual adaptation as a response to evolving attacks, while preserving the distinction between measured attack resistance and the broader goal of safer open-ended deployment.
neurips-2025-lifelong-safety-alignment-f.tldr: A continually trained attacker–defender framework improves jailbreak resistance, reducing the reported Meta-Attacker success rate to 7%.

paragraphs: Widely circulated mathematics benchmarks make it difficult to separate reasoning ability from possible exposure to the problems during training. MathArena uses recurring competitions as a source of new, challenging questions. By evaluating models immediately after problems are released, the framework is designed to remove contamination risk through the timing of evaluation.

The benchmark also evaluates proof writing, extending assessment beyond tasks that only require an answer. At the point described in the paper, the authors have evaluated more than 50 models across seven competitions containing 162 problems. The ongoing stream of competition problems allows the evaluation to keep changing as models improve.

The analysis finds strong signs of contamination in AIME 2024, while performance on harder competitions such as CMIMC 2025 still demonstrates impressive reasoning in leading models. On IMO 2025, the top models achieve slightly less than 40%, showing both progress and substantial remaining difficulty in proof writing. These findings make problem freshness and proof-based evaluation complementary ways to assess mathematical capability more meaningfully.
neurips-2025-matharena-evaluating-llms-o.tldr: MathArena evaluates models on newly released math competitions and proofs, finding strong reasoning alongside contamination concerns and substantial remaining proof-writing difficulty.

paragraphs: Visual neural activity reflects both what an animal sees and its internal state. A model driven only by video therefore leaves out another source of variation in neuronal responses. This paper introduces a probabilistic model that combines naturalistic video stimuli with latent factors representing influences independent of the stimulus.

The model predicts the joint distribution of neuronal responses, allowing it to describe population activity rather than only a single predicted response for each neuron. On mouse V1 recordings, it achieves better log-likelihood than video-only models. Conditioning on responses from other neurons further improves likelihood and correlation, showing the value of incorporating information from the neural population.

The learned latent factors strongly correlate with mouse behavior and show patterns related to neurons' positions on the visual cortex. Neither behavior nor cortical coordinates was supplied during training. These associations suggest that unsupervised learning from population responses can recover biologically meaningful structure linking sensory activity and behavior. The findings concern discovered correlations and spatial patterns, which explain why the latent factors are informative beyond their predictive contribution.
neurips-2025-modeling-dynamic-neural-act.tldr: Combining video with learned latent factors improves neural-response prediction and reveals behavioral and cortical associations without those annotations during training.

paragraphs: This paper studies mechanisms for maximizing utility when buyers value multiple different items but each buyer demands at most one. Its setting assumes values are independent and identically distributed across both buyers and items. The goal is to understand how well simple mechanisms can perform relative to optimal social welfare, which serves as an upper benchmark.

The authors construct approximately optimal mechanisms that do not require knowledge of the value distribution. When items outnumber buyers, they obtain a one-minus-one-over-e approximation to welfare. When buyers outnumber items, the approximation factor has logarithmic order in the ratio of buyers to items. These results extend earlier analysis of identical items to a multidimensional valuation setting.

A reduction to the identical-item setting establishes tightness in both the number of buyers and the number of items. The paper also examines why utility maximization behaves differently from the more familiar welfare and revenue objectives. Its discussion emphasizes that selecting a benchmark better suited than welfare is itself difficult, making the benchmark question part of the research contribution.
neurips-2025-multidimensional-bayesian-u.tldr: Under i.i.d. unit-demand values, the paper gives simple prior-independent utility mechanisms with tight welfare-approximation guarantees.

paragraphs: Goal-conditioned reinforcement learning learns how to reach a requested state. Two successful approaches represent this problem differently: contrastive methods learn about future outcomes, while temporal-distance methods represent how long reaching a goal should take. This paper combines those approaches in a single representation-learning objective for learning from offline data.

The method uses a quasimetric space whose distances satisfy the triangle inequality, together with additional constraints. That structure supports stitching together parts of the available experience into goal-reaching behavior. The authors show that the resulting successor representations can learn optimal goal-reaching distances even when the data are suboptimal and the environment is stochastic.

The combination is intended to preserve the stability and long-horizon strengths of Monte Carlo contrastive learning while gaining the stitching abilities of quasimetric networks. On existing offline benchmarks, the objective improves performance on stitching tasks that challenge contrastive methods and on noisy, high-dimensional environments that challenge quasimetric methods. The findings support combining the two representation structures to address complementary weaknesses in the tested settings.
neurips-2025-offline-goal-conditioned-re.tldr: A unified contrastive and quasimetric representation learns optimal goal-reaching distances from suboptimal offline data and improves performance on complementary benchmark challenges.

paragraphs: Structured pruning removes model weights according to a prescribed sparsity pattern. Reordering the channels of a weight matrix can help important weights survive that process, but choosing a good ordering is difficult. PermLLM replaces handcrafted measures of ordering quality with a learnable channel-permutation procedure for N:M sparse language models.

The key obstacle is that permutations are discrete, making them difficult to optimize directly with gradients. PermLLM uses Sinkhorn normalization to form differentiable soft permutation matrices, enabling end-to-end optimization. It also organizes channel permutations block by block, reducing the number of learnable parameters and the computational complexity of the optimization.

The framework operates after training and integrates with existing one-shot pruning methods. Its purpose is to adapt channel orderings in ways that reduce errors introduced by pruning, rather than relying only on a manually chosen proxy for which arrangement is best. Experiments on the LLaMA series, Qwen, and OPT report superior performance in optimizing N:M sparse models, supporting learned channel arrangement as a useful component of post-training compression.
neurips-2025-permllm-learnable-channel-p.tldr: PermLLM learns channel reorderings through differentiable soft permutations to reduce errors from structured language-model pruning.

paragraphs: Secure aggregation systems combine high-dimensional vectors while protecting individual contributions. In private federated learning, those vectors can be gradients, with added noise protecting the aggregate through differential privacy. Existing two-server approaches require communication that grows with vector dimensionality, limiting how efficiently they can handle large vectors.

PREAMBLE develops an extension of distributed point functions for block-sparse vectors. These vectors have nonzero entries concentrated in a small number of consecutive groups of coordinates. Exploiting that structure enables more efficient communication and computation during aggregation. The method combines this representation with random sampling and privacy amplification from sampling.

The analysis establishes asymptotically optimal privacy–utility trade-offs while using a fraction of the communication cost. Combined with recent numerical privacy-accounting methods, PREAMBLE adds only negligible noise-variance overhead relative to the Gaussian mechanism used with Prio. The significance is the combination of reduced communication and a favorable privacy–utility trade-off within the studied two-server aggregation setup, rather than treating lower communication as a reason to accept substantially noisier results.
neurips-2025-preamble-private-and-effici.tldr: PREAMBLE uses block-sparse representations and sampling to reduce secure-aggregation communication while preserving asymptotically optimal privacy–utility trade-offs.

paragraphs: Designing a protein from a textual description requires both matching the requested function and producing a structurally plausible sequence. Existing generative approaches can struggle with the structural side. This paper explores using fragments from natural proteins as building material, finding empirically that even randomly incorporating such fragments improves foldability.

ProDVa builds on that observation with a more targeted system. A text encoder represents the requested function, a protein language model generates sequences, and a fragment encoder dynamically retrieves protein fragments according to the functional description. This gives generation access to natural protein pieces selected in relation to the design request.

The experiments report function alignment comparable to state-of-the-art models while using less than 0.04% of their training data and generating more well-folded proteins. The reported proportions meeting pLDDT above 70 and PAE below 10 increase by 7.38% and 9.62%, respectively. These findings support fragment retrieval as a way to improve structural plausibility while retaining alignment with textual function descriptions in the evaluated designs.
neurips-2025-protein-design-with-dynamic.tldr: ProDVa retrieves natural protein fragments from functional descriptions, improving reported structural plausibility while matching function alignment with far less training data.

paragraphs: Generating several candidate answers can improve language-model reasoning, but the system still needs to choose among them. Reward models add evaluation cost, while agreement-based alternatives can struggle with open-ended answers. This paper proposes self-certainty, a response-quality metric derived from the language model's own output probability distribution.

The central hypothesis is that greater distributional self-certainty, aggregated across samples, correlates with greater answer accuracy. The metric uses that signal to support best-of-N selection without an external reward model. It therefore connects the extra computation spent generating candidates to a selection procedure based on information already present in the model's outputs.

Experiments across reasoning tasks show that self-certainty remains effective as the number of candidates grows, with scaling behavior resembling reward-based selection without its external evaluation overhead. It also improves chain-of-thought reasoning beyond greedy decoding and extends to open-ended tasks where traditional self-consistency falls short. The evidence supports self-certainty as a useful empirical selection signal; the confidence–accuracy relationship remains the hypothesis motivating the method.
neurips-2025-scalable-best-of-n-selectio.tldr: Self-certainty uses a language model's output probabilities to select among candidate answers, improving reported reasoning without an external reward model.

paragraphs: Time series can reflect hidden processes organized into several levels, with each level contributing to the observed dynamics. Recovering that hierarchy is difficult when only one timestep's observations are used. This paper finds that three conditionally independent observations can uniquely determine the joint distribution of hierarchical latent variables, providing a foundation for its identification framework.

CHiLD first uses observed temporal context to identify the joint distribution across latent layers. It then exploits sparsity in the hierarchical structure to identify variables within each layer. These are distinct parts of the task: recovering how hidden variables behave jointly and distinguishing the variables that make up each level.

Guided by the theory, the authors construct a generative time-series model using variational inference. A contextual encoder reconstructs the multilayer latent variables, while normalizing-flow hierarchical prior networks impose the independent-noise condition. Evaluations on synthetic and real-world datasets support the theoretical claims and demonstrate effective modeling of hierarchical dynamics. The conditional independence and structural properties are central to the identification argument, rather than incidental implementation details.
neurips-2025-towards-identifiability-of-.tldr: CHiLD uses temporal context, conditional independence, and hierarchical sparsity to identify and model multiple layers of hidden time-series dynamics.

paragraphs: Long-context language models must retain substantial information in their key-value cache, creating a memory bottleneck. Compressing sequences can reduce that burden, but it risks discarding details needed later. UniGist addresses this tension with gist tokens and a training framework that teaches the model both to compress long context and to use the compressed information.

The framework removes the need for chunk-wise training and supports training in one pass. On the computation side, a gist-shift technique reorganizes attention into a right-aligned block layout. A sparse attention kernel designed for that layout avoids using a block table, connecting the compression structure to an implementation that can exploit its sparsity.

UniGist also permits flexible chunk sizes at inference, allowing context processing to adapt after training. Across multiple long-context tasks, the authors report significantly improved compression quality, especially for recalling details and handling long-range dependencies. The contribution combines a learning approach for preserving useful information with an attention layout and kernel designed to make the compressed representation computationally useful.
neurips-2025-unigist-towards-general-and.tldr: UniGist combines gist-token training with specialized sparse attention to improve long-context compression, particularly detail recall and long-range dependency modeling.

paragraphs: Selection bias appears when observed data reflect selective behavior, such as users choosing which items to interact with. Doubly robust estimators are widely used to correct this bias. This paper examines an additional problem: existing approaches assume the same individual units appear in training and testing, although real datasets may contain little or no overlap.

The authors instead assume that training and test data share the joint distribution of features and ratings. Under this setting, they show that the previous doubly robust estimator remains biased even when its imputed errors and learned observation propensities are correct. The issue therefore involves how the datasets relate, beyond the accuracy of those correction components.

The proposed SuperDR estimator is designed for this population-based setting, with improved estimation and a favorable generalization-error bound compared with existing doubly robust estimators. The paper also extends joint training of the prediction and imputation models. Experiments on three real-world datasets, including a large industrial dataset, support its effectiveness. The contribution clarifies why correcting selective observations also requires accounting for sampling differences between training and evaluation units.
neurips-2025-unveiling-extraneous-sampli.tldr: SuperDR addresses bias that persists in existing doubly robust estimators when training and test units differ despite sharing a feature–rating distribution.

paragraphs: Web agents can carry out tasks on a user's behalf, so malicious instructions encountered during browsing can affect real actions. WASP evaluates this threat through end-to-end prompt-injection scenarios. It is designed to improve on tests that simplify the environment, give attackers unrealistic control, or examine only an isolated step.

The benchmark follows attacks through the broader task, allowing evaluation to distinguish influencing an agent from completing an attacker's objective. Tests show that even leading models with advanced reasoning capabilities can be deceived by simple human-written injections in realistic scenarios. The attack does not need to be elaborate to affect the agent's behavior in these evaluations.

Partial attack success reaches as high as 86% of cases, yet agents often fail to finish the attacker's full goal. The paper describes this gap as security arising from incompetence: incomplete malicious outcomes can reflect limited execution ability even when the injection has already worked. This finding makes end-to-end evaluation especially informative because it separates resistance to manipulation from failure to carry out the resulting actions.
neurips-2025-wasp-benchmarking-web-agent.tldr: WASP finds that realistic prompt injections often partially succeed, while limited agent execution ability frequently prevents completion of the attacker's full goal.
